props.title: Little Murders
props.initialSlug: Dark comedy about NYC couple amid urban chaos

sections.content: Little Murders represents a pivotal moment in dark American comedy, capturing the paranoid zeitgeist of early 1970s New York City. Directed by Alan Arkin and adapted from Jules Feiffer's play, this caustic satire follows photographer Alfred (Elliott Gould) and his relationship with eternal optimist Patsy (Marcia Rodd) against a backdrop of random violence, urban decay, and societal collapse. The film shares DNA with other early '70s chronicles of urban anxiety like The Taking of Pelham One Two Three (1974) and The Out of Towners (1970), but pushes further into absurdist territory.

sections.content: The film's unflinching examination of violence and alienation in urban America places it alongside other early '70s works grappling with similar themes through different genres. While Taxi Driver (1976) approached urban decay through psychological thriller elements and Death Wish (1974) through vigilante action, Little Murders uses pitch-black comedy to expose society's absurdities. The film's innovative blend of stage and screen techniques influenced later works like After Hours (1985) and Quick Change (1990).

What sets Little Murders apart is its prescient understanding of how violence becomes normalized. The random shootings, power outages, and general breakdown of civil society depicted feel eerily contemporary. The film's influence can be traced through later urban paranoia comedies like After Hours (1985) and Quick Change (1990), while its mixing of comedy with genuine dread prefigures work by the Coen Brothers, particularly The Big Lebowski (1998). sections.content: The film's DNA can be found in modern dark comedies that mix absurdism with social commentary. World's Greatest Dad (2009) and God Bless America (2011) share its willingness to push comedy to uncomfortable places, while Promising Young Woman (2020) echoes its examination of violence and gender dynamics through a similarly pitch-black lens. The film's influence extends to television series like "Search Party" and "Barry," which similarly blend comedy with darkness and urban paranoia.
